subtitle: When the Throne Became a Stage

panels.shot: low-angle wide of a dim royal chamber, half throne room, half theatre, scrolls and masks scattered around a seated king
panels.action: Harsha sits between his jeweled throne and a low writing desk, one hand on a sword, the other on a palm-leaf manuscript, as shadowy actors in the background hold masks of kings, nagas, and lovers.

dialogue.text: In the age of Kannauj, an emperor lays aside his sword to write a play where a king chooses compassion over conquest.

i18n.hi: कन्नौज के युग में सम्राट तलवार छोड़, नाटक लिखता है जहाँ राजा जीत नहीं, दया चुनता है।

panels.shot: bird’s-eye view over the Ganga plain, then down into the bustling city of Kannauj
panels.action: The camera swoops from the hazy Ganga floodplain into the crowded streets and high terraces of Kannauj, where Harsha stands on a balcony looking over temples, markets and caravan routes.

dialogue.text: Seventh-century Kannauj, crossroads of the plains, feels the weight of an empire and the hum of many faiths: Shaiva temples, Buddhist monasteries, shrines of many gods.

i18n.hi: सातवीं सदी का कन्नौज, राहों का चौराहा; साम्राज्य का भार, और कई धर्मों की गूँज: शैव देवालय, बौद्ध विहार, कई देवों के थान।

panels.shot: medium close-up of Harsha in court, ministers and brahmanas on one side, monks and envoys on the other
panels.action: Harsha sits on his ornate lion throne, flanked by brahman advisors with copper plates and Buddhist monks with folded hands, as foreign envoys watch in curiosity.

dialogue.text: Copper plates call him a Shaiva ruler; Chinese records praise his patronage of monasteries. In this court, the emperor hears many creeds, and must be seen by all.

i18n.hi: ताम्रपत्र उसे शैव नरेश कहते हैं; चीनी वृत्त उसे विहारों का दानी। इस दरबार में सम्राट कई मत सुनता है, और सबकी नज़र में रहता है।

panels.shot: intimate interior, candlelit, slow push-in on Harsha alone at night
panels.action: By lamplight in a quieter chamber, Harsha leans over palm-leaf manuscripts, a stylus in hand, walls lined with neatly stacked bundles of texts.

dialogue.text: In this age, kings sponsor poets. Yet tradition whispers a different tale: that Harsha himself composed three courtly plays.

i18n.hi: इन दिनों राजा कवियों को पालते हैं। पर परंपरा एक और कथा फुसफुसाती है: कि हर्ष ने खुद तीन नाटक रचे।

panels.shot: over-the-shoulder close-up of palm leaf where the name ‘Nagananda’ would be, though no letters are shown
panels.action: Over Harsha’s shoulder, we see his hand pause above the palm leaf as he thinks, a faint smile forming, while a mask of a serpent-headed being rests beside the manuscript.

dialogue.text: Nagananda, Ratnavali, Priyadarsika. Later ages will debate if these were truly his, or the work of a court poet like Dhavaka named in the Kavyaprakasha.

i18n.hi: नागानन्द, रत्नावली, प्रीयदर्शिका। बाद के युग बहस करेंगे—ये सच में उसी के हैं, या किसी धवक जैसे दरबारी कवि के, जिसका नाम काव्यप्रकाश में है।

panels.shot: medium shot, Harsha dictating, scribes seated below taking down his words
panels.action: Harsha stands, gesturing with controlled energy, as two scribes sit cross-legged, scratching lines onto fresh leaves, listening keenly.

dialogue.speaker: harsha
dialogue.text: “Let the stage be our mirror. Let kings see themselves there.”

i18n.hi: “मंच को हमारा आईना बनाओ। राजा खुद को वहीं देखें।”

panels.shot: mythic montage, wide, blending stage and legend
panels.action: On a simple wooden stage within the palace, actors in colorful costumes play out a scene: a noble hero Jimutavahana stands firm, a stylized naga coiled beside him, and a looming figure of a bird-like demon hovers in the backdrop.

dialogue.text: Nagananda tells of Jimutavahana, who offers his own body to save a naga from a garuda’s hunger; a prince who lays down his life instead of taking another’s.

i18n.hi: नागानन्द में जिमुतवाहन अपनी देह दे देता है, ताकि गरुड़ के पंजे से नाग बच जाए; राजकुमार जो अपनी जान देता है, किसी और की नहीं लेता।

panels.shot: close-up on a manuscript colophon space, half-shadowed, hinting at ambiguous authorship
panels.action: A palm-leaf manuscript lies open, with an ornamental ending line and empty space where a signature might be, while a scholar’s fingertip hovers over it.

dialogue.text: The play’s benediction honors the Buddha. Yet the manuscript keeps its secrets; no line within settles whose hand shaped these verses.

i18n.hi: नाटक की मंगल-श्लोक बुद्ध को नमन् करती है। पर पांडुलिपि चुप रहती है; कोई पंक्ति नहीं बताती कि इन श्लोकों को किसने गढ़ा।

panels.shot: profile shot of Harsha listening to a brahmana and a monk debating, with the distant sound of rehearsal
panels.action: In a corridor, Harsha pauses between a brahmana quoting a Shaiva hymn and a monk reciting a Buddhist stanza, while from a nearby hall actors practice gestures.

dialogue.text: Harsha’s own grants use Shaiva titles. Yet a play from his court opens with homage to the Buddha, and moves with the rhythms of Sanskrit theatre known to brahmana and monk alike.

i18n.hi: हर्ष के अपने दान-पत्र शैव उपाधियाँ रखते हैं। फिर भी उसके दरबार का नाटक बुद्ध वंदना से शुरू होता है, और संस्कृत रंगमंच की वही लय चलती है जिसे ब्राह्मण और भिक्षु दोनों जानते हैं।

panels.shot: crisp medium shot in rehearsal hall, Harsha watching actors perform a key Nagananda scene
panels.action: Harsha sits on a simple chair at the side of a rehearsal hall, intent as an actor portraying Jimutavahana kneels in calm resolve, a cloth garland ready in his hands.

dialogue.speaker: harsha
dialogue.text: “Hold that stillness. Let them feel his choice before he speaks.”

i18n.hi: “उस स्थिरता को पकड़े रखो। वे उसकी चॉइस महसूस करें, बोलने से पहले।”

panels.shot: dramatic tight shot on the actor-Jimutavahana’s face, lit from above, stage behind in shadow
panels.action: The actor playing Jimutavahana looks upward in serene determination, hands folded, as a feathered garuda mask hangs ominously in the background.

dialogue.text: On stage, Jimutavahana lies down beneath the beak of death. The hero is not the conqueror, but the one who refuses to let another die in his place.

i18n.hi: मंच पर जिमुतवाहन मौत की चोंच के नीचे लेट जाता है। नायक वह है जो जीतता नहीं, जो किसी और को मरने नहीं देता।

panels.shot: wide shot of palace theatre filled with courtiers, Harsha in the royal box
panels.action: The court theatre is packed with jeweled nobles, scholars and envoys, all eyes on the stage, as Harsha watches from a slightly elevated box, arms folded tightly.

dialogue.text: When the play is performed, the court must meet this question: what if a king chose sacrifice over cruelty, mercy over the easy order of violence?

i18n.hi: जब नाटक खेला जाता है, दरबार को इस सवाल से भिड़ना पड़ता है: अगर राजा बलि चुने, क्रूरता नहीं? दया चुने, हिंसा का आसान हुक्म नहीं?

panels.shot: montage-like wide shot showing another play, Ratnavali, in performance with a spring festival scene
panels.action: On the same stage, actors in a different play frolic as they throw colored powders and sprinkle water, trees budding with new leaves painted on the backdrop, while a heroine laughs shyly behind a veil.

dialogue.text: In Ratnavali, another drama from this circle, the stage blossoms with a spring festival of colors, among the earliest Sanskrit scenes that later readers link with Holi.

i18n.hi: रत्नावली में, इसी मंडली का दूसरा नाटक, मंच पर रंगों से भरा बसंतोत्सव खिलता है—सबसे शुरुआती संस्कृत दृश्यों में, जिन्हें बाद के पाठक होली से जोड़ते हैं।

panels.shot: medium shot of Ratnavali’s romantic court scene, blending politics and love
panels.action: An actor king in Ratnavali stands between a queen and the witty heroine Ratnavali, courtiers watching, as a jester peeks from behind a pillar.

dialogue.text: Here, the drama plays with mistaken identities, palace intrigue and the pull of desire, showing another face of power: tender, scheming, entangled in the everyday.

i18n.hi: यहाँ नाटक उलटी-पुलटी पहचान, महल की साज़िश और चाह की खींच से खेलता है; शक्ति का दूसरा चेहरा दिखता है—नरम, चालाक, रोज़मर्रा में उलझा।

panels.shot: serene medium shot of Harsha after a performance, walking slowly through an emptied hall
panels.action: After the audience has gone, Harsha walks alone across the now-empty stage, lightly touching a discarded mask of a king before setting it down.

dialogue.speaker: harsha
dialogue.text: “On this floor, even emperors are made of painted wood and words.”

i18n.hi: “इस फर्श पर सम्राट भी बस रंग, लकड़ी और शब्द हैं।”

panels.shot: time-lapse style wide shot of manuscripts being copied over generations
panels.action: The image shows successive scenes of scribes in different centuries copying the same style of palm-leaf manuscripts, stacks growing, while outside architecture slowly changes.

dialogue.text: Whatever his hand in their making, these plays travel beyond Kannauj: copied by scribes, quoted by critics, staged and restaged in courts and schools.

i18n.hi: चाहे उसकी कलम जितनी भी लगी हो, ये नाटक कन्नौज से परे निकल जाते हैं: नकलची लिखते हैं, आलोचक उद्धृत करते हैं, दरबारों और पाठशालाओं में बार-बार खेले जाते हैं।

panels.shot: modern-era scholar’s desk wide shot, manuscripts and printed editions open together
panels.action: A modern scholar sits at a cluttered desk, with an old manuscript facsimile beside printed editions of Nagananda, Ratnavali and Priyadarsika, annotating with care.

dialogue.text: Later scholars argue over authorship, weigh styles, compare inscriptions and treatises, and keep the question open rather than forcing the past into a simple answer.

i18n.hi: बाद के पंडित लेखन पर झगड़ते हैं, शैलियाँ तौलते हैं, शिलालेख और शास्त्र मिलाते हैं, और जवाब थोपने से बेहतर सवाल खुला रखते हैं।

panels.shot: final reflective medium-close on Harsha, half in shadow, looking toward an unseen stage
panels.action: Harsha stands at the edge of the darkened theatre, face lit by a faint glow from the stage, expression thoughtful, as if listening to echoes of dialogue.

dialogue.text: In the memory of Nagananda’s self-offering and Ratnavali’s festival of color, power is asked a quiet question: will you rule by fear alone, or dare to answer to compassion as well?

i18n.hi: नागानन्द की आत्मबलि और रत्नावली के रंगोत्सव की याद में, सत्ता से एक धीमा सवाल होता है: क्या तुम सिर्फ डर से राज करोगे, या करुणा को भी जवाब दोगे?

subtitle_i18n.en: When the Throne Became a Stage
